1:
The witnesses open the chapter by reckoning its date and reading the long, deliberate pause that lies behind it. The reformed John Gill and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott both notice that though Nisan — the old Abib, the first month of the Jewish year after the vernal equinox — fell later than the Chisleu of the previous chapter, the text still calls it the twentieth year of Artaxerxes. Gill explains that while the Jews dated their kings' reigns from Nisan, other nations began them from Tisri, so that the two months could fall within a single regnal year; Ellicott agrees that the record adopts Persian dates, and that the reign must therefore have begun before Chisleu.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fastens on the nearly four months that passed from Chisleu to Nisan, between the first tidings of Jerusalem's ruin and Nehemiah's approach to the king. He will not read the delay as sloth. When Nehemiah had prayed — perhaps in David's words, "build thou the walls of Jerusalem," from Ps. 51:18 — he did not sit still and say the work was God's alone, but set himself to forecast what he could do; "our prayers must be seconded with our serious endeavours, else we mock God." The delay itself, Henry supposes, was because winter was no season for such a journey, or because it was long before his month of waiting came round, since none might enter the king's presence uncalled, as Esther 4:11 shows. Now that he attended the king's table, he hoped to have his ear.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill in the same picture. John Wesley likewise dates it four months after the sad news, and lays the delay either to Nehemiah's turn of attendance not coming till then or to his waiting for a fit opportunity to move the matter. Adam Clarke supplies the courtly detail: the kings of Persia, he notes, are supposed to have kept a different cup-bearer for each quarter of the year, and it had just now come to Nehemiah's turn to serve, when he took up the wine and gave it to the king. Gill adds that the intervening months may well have been spent in the fasting and prayer with which the previous chapter had closed. The voices do not divide; together they set before us a patient courtier who has prayed and waited, and now, wine in hand, seizes the first opening providence affords to plead for the city of his fathers.
2:
The king's abrupt question — "Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick?" — and Nehemiah's sudden dread are what the witnesses gather to explain. The reformed John Gill notes the plain fact that startles Artaxerxes: Nehemiah had no bodily disorder to account for the change in his face, and so the king asks the reason. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the king's own diagnosis — "this is nothing else but sorrow of heart" — and mark that Nehemiah, though very sore afraid, nevertheless openly expressed his desire, prefacing it with the accustomed wish of prosperity, "let the king live for ever," a formula they set beside Daniel 2:4.

Over the cause of that fear the witnesses genuinely differ. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, suspects the king spoke as one who half-feared some bad design, as if the sad face betrayed conceived treachery or remorse. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, traces the fear rather to the suddenness of the inquiry: Nehemiah had discharged his duties three months without being sad in the royal presence, but on this day his sorrow could not be repressed, and a sad countenance was never tolerated before the king; even the milder Artaxerxes, whose tone showed him no exception to the rule, made the moment perilous. The other wesleyan voice, John Wesley, reads the fear differently again: his fasting joined with inward grief had wrought a visible change in his face, and he was afraid because it was an unusual and ungrateful thing to appear sorrowful before a Persian king, and because his request was great and invidious, odious to most of the courtiers, so that he dreaded a refusal.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds a fourth reading and draws the lesson. Though the sequel proves Nehemiah a man of courage, he was now sorely afraid — perhaps of the king's wrath, for those eastern monarchs claimed an absolute power of life and death, as Daniel 2:12 and 5:19 attest, or of misplacing a word and losing his suit by mismanaging it. A wise man, Henry observes, may yet be jealous of himself lest he speak imprudently, and a humble self-diffidence is no man's dispraise. On the king's side Henry commends the tender notice taken of a servant's grief: we ought, from Christian sympathy, to concern ourselves in the sorrows even of our inferiors, and not to say, "What is it to us?" The voices converge on the picture of a frightened but resolute man, and part only over what most frightened him — suspicion, protocol, the greatness of his request, or the peril of a single ill-chosen word.
3:
Nehemiah's reply frames his grief so as to disarm suspicion and to touch the one chord a Persian would feel — the honour of the dead. The reformed John Gill reads the opening blessing, "let the king live for ever," as at once a common courtly salutation and, some think, a deliberate stroke to take off any suspicion that he had designs upon the king's life. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, hears the same disclaimer — far from wishing his master ill, Nehemiah wishes him to live and prosper for ever — and finds the very form elsewhere: Aelian records the greeting offered to Artaxerxes Mnemon, "O King Artaxerxes, may you reign for ever," used as the Persians presented their yearly offering of earth and water.

On the substance of the answer the witnesses agree that Nehemiah is careful and shrewd. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, notes that his family was of Jerusalem, and that he does not yet betray to the king the deepest desire of his heart, but simply pleads the desecration of his fathers' sepulchres — an appeal of great force with the Persians, who held the tomb in reverence. The other wesleyan voice, John Wesley, sharpens the same observation into a rule of prudence: Nehemiah's sadness, he says, sprang not from any disaffection to the king, for whom his hearty prayers were that he might live for ever, but from another cause; and, speaking before a heathen king who cared for none of these things, he said not a word of the temple, naming only the sepulchres, which all nations esteem sacred and inviolable.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry justifies the grief itself and gathers the lesson. Nehemiah calls Jerusalem the place of his fathers' sepulchres, and it is good, Henry says, to think often of our fathers' graves; we dwell readily on their honours and estates, but their monuments are mementos to us, and there is a great respect owing to their memory. Nehemiah does not merely mourn but vindicates his mourning — "I do well to be sad; why should I not be so?" — for there is a time even for pious and prosperous men to grieve, and the desolations of Jerusalem are cause enough. All the grievances of the church, Henry insists, and above all its ruins, ought to be matter of grief to every good soul that has a public spirit and favours even Zion's dust. The witnesses do not divide; they show a man who guards his safety, honours his dead, and lays the ruin of the holy city before a pagan throne in terms that throne could not despise.
4:
The king's open invitation — "For what dost thou make request?" — and Nehemiah's instantaneous, silent prayer draw every witness to the same wonder: a petition to the God of heaven slipped in between a question and its answer. The reformed John Gill takes the king to have supposed there was a meaning in those sad looks, some favour to be asked, and so to have encouraged his servant to name it, being himself desirous to set him at ease. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the question as a sign that the king was already inclined to relieve the distress of Jerusalem just laid before him; and Nehemiah, before laying his request in words, "prayed to the God of heaven," to secure divine help for what he was about to ask.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, marks the nature of that prayer: before he dared prefer his suit to the king, Nehemiah made his prayer to God, and this by mental prayer only — "to the spirit of prayer every place is a praying place." Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, calls it the first note of that habit of ejaculatory prayer which is a characteristic of the whole book. The other wesleyan voice, John Wesley, states its double aim: he prayed to direct his own thoughts and words, and to incline the king's heart to grant his request.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers longest and turns the moment into instruction. The king had an affection for Nehemiah and, wishing only to know how he might serve Jerusalem, drew him out; and this invitation gave him boldness where a moment before he had been afraid to speak — "much more may the invitation Christ has given us to pray, and the promise that we shall speed, enable us to come boldly to the throne of grace." Nehemiah immediately lifted up his heart to the God of heaven, infinitely above even this mighty monarch, in a secret sudden ejaculation: "Lord, give me a mouth and wisdom; Lord, give me favour in the sight of this man." He had already prayed solemnly for this very occasion in the previous chapter, yet when it comes to the push he prays again, for ejaculations and solemn prayers must not jostle out one another, but each keep its place. Those, Henry concludes, who would find favour with kings must first secure the favour of the King of kings. The witnesses stand as one: the whole business turned on a prayer no one at the table could hear.
5:
With the king's ear won and heaven's help sought, Nehemiah at last names his errand, and the witnesses weigh the modesty and the boldness mingled in it. The reformed John Gill observes how he frames the petition: he submits it wholly to the king's pleasure and rests it on unmerited favour, not on any desert of his own — "if it please the king, and if thy servant have found favour in thy sight." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the request it introduces: that the king would send him to Judah, to the city of his fathers' sepulchres, that he might build it; the conditional courtesy, they note, is the same idiom of finding favour "before" the king that recurs in the book of Esther. The very form of the sentence, they observe, joins the matter of the request directly to that humble condition, so that Nehemiah asks nothing until he has first cast himself upon the king's goodwill.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, returns to the shrewdness of the plea. By naming again "the city of my fathers' sepulchres," Nehemiah touched a chord certain to move a Persian: the tombs of the dead were sacred among the ancients, and nothing could seem to them more detestable than disturbing the ashes or remains of the departed; Nehemiah knew that in urging this he would strongly interest the feelings of the king.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds all that the modest words in fact contained. Nehemiah asked, in effect, for a commission to go as governor to Judah, to build the wall of Jerusalem, and to remain there a set term — so many months, we may suppose, after which his commission was renewed or he was sent again, for he presided in Judah twelve years at least, as Nehemiah 5:14 records. That the request touched the very walls which adversaries had, in an earlier reign, gotten the work stopped upon as seditious only magnifies the wonder that the king should now authorize their rebuilding. He asked, too, for more than leave to go: a convoy for the road and letters of authority to the governors, which the following verses will detail. Henry marvels that so large a request, touching the fortification of a city once charged with sedition, should be granted at all, and traces it not to Nehemiah's interest at court nor to his own management but to the good hand of his God upon him. The witnesses do not divide; together they show a petition humble in its form and vast in its content — a captive cup-bearer asking, and receiving, the governorship of a province and the rebuilding of its ruined capital, because the God of heaven had gone before him into the king's heart.
6:
The scene widens to include the queen at the king's side, and the witnesses read both the unusual company and the providence in it. The reformed John Gill notes that it was not common for the queens of Persia to dine with their husbands, and marks the hand of God in her presence, for she bore a good will to Nehemiah and the Jewish nation and helped forward the king's grant; were this king Darius Hystaspis, he guesses, the queen would be Atossa the daughter of Cyrus, the more friendly to the Jews for her father's sake. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply record that king and queen — the shegal of Psalms 45:9 — granted Nehemiah leave once he had, at their asking, fixed the length of his absence, so that "it pleased the king to send me."

Here the witnesses divide over who this royal woman was. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, denies that she was the queen at all: the word shegal does not properly mean queen but rather the chief favourite or concubine, which the Septuagint renders bluntly; and she was certainly not Esther, against Dean Prideaux. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, takes the opposite view — she was probably Damaspia, the one legitimate queen — and adds that this was no public feast, for at such the queen would not have been present, as the book of Esther shows in Esther 1:9. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, is content to note her presence as unusual, since the kings of Persia commonly dined alone, and to suppose that she expressed some kindness and promoted the request.

On the king's question — "For how long shall thy journey be? and when wilt thou return?" — the witnesses hear affection. It showed, Wesley says, that the king was unwilling to be long without his attendance; and the "time" Nehemiah set was, Clarke reckons, perhaps six months or a year, though circumstances afterward stretched it, for in the same year he was made governor and continued twelve years, as Nehemiah 5:14 attests, and the wall itself was raised in the fifty-two days of Nehemiah 6:15. Clarke traces the sequel further still: Nehemiah returned to the king after his term and was later sent back to redress the abuses that Tobiah had brought into the temple, as Nehemiah 13:6 records; Wesley too supposes that not long after the wall was finished he returned to court, whence the king sent him a second time with a fuller commission. Ellicott agrees the term, whatever it was, was later prolonged. The voices differ only on the queen's title and station, and agree on the providence — that a foreign court, wife beside king, was moved to send a Jewish captive home to build.
7:
Nehemiah's foresight now shows itself: leave to go is not enough without safe passage and supply, and the witnesses attend to the requests he adds. The reformed John Gill identifies the "river" of the petition as the Euphrates, and the governors "beyond the river" as those on the side of it toward the land of Judah, through whose provinces Nehemiah's road would run. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the request in order: Nehemiah asked for letters to these governors west of the Euphrates, that they might grant him unmolested passage through their territories until he came into Judah, and — as the next verse will add — a further letter to the keeper of the royal forests; and both requests, they note, were granted.

Charles Ellicott, also grammatical-historical, adds a shrewd geographical qualification. Nehemiah sought protection only for the stretch beyond the river, because "between the Euphrates and Susa protection was not needed" — the danger lay in the western provinces near his goal, not in the settled heart of the empire through which he first must travel. The letters, then, were not a courtier's excess of caution but a precise provision for the one part of the journey where a returning Jew, bent on refortifying Jerusalem, might meet obstruction. The observation is a fine instance of his attention to the map of empire: a returning exile needed no safe-conduct among the loyal heart-provinces, but every warrant he could get among the restless satrapies that ringed his homeland.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse rewards their brevity with a lesson in prudent faith. Nehemiah had prayed and had trusted the good hand of his God; yet he neglected no lawful means, but secured in writing the cooperation of every official whose province he must cross and whose goodwill or ill-will could speed or hinder the work. He asked the king not merely to release him but to arm him with authority, so that the governors who might have questioned or delayed a solitary traveller would instead be bound to convey him on his way. That he could command such letters at all presupposes the commission just granted, the captive cup-bearer now clothed with the standing of a royal envoy. Trust in providence and diligence in arrangement, the witnesses show, walked together in this man; and the same king who had granted the errand now furnished the safe-conducts that made it possible, the good hand of God moving through the ordinary channels of royal letters and provincial duty. He would arrive in Judah not as a suppliant begging leave of suspicious officials but as a man whose passage they were commanded to further, and his enemies would learn soon enough that he came with the empire's writ behind him.
8:
The last of Nehemiah's requests concerns the timber for the work, and the witnesses divide pleasantly over where the wood was to come from before uniting on the confession that crowns the verse. The reformed John Gill takes Asaph to have kept the forest or mountain of Lebanon, so rich in fragrant and fruit-bearing trees that the word used for it means an orchard or paradise; such an officer, he adds, the Romans called a saltuarius. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, agrees that it was the forest of Lebanon, famous for its choice trees, and reads the "palace" for whose gates the beams were wanted as the king's palace adjoining the house of God, with a further grant of timber for the house Nehemiah himself should build to dwell in.

Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, dissents on both points. Asaph, he holds, was a Jew who kept an artificial park or pleasure-ground near Jerusalem — the Persian pardes, whence our word "paradise" — well planted with timber; and the beams were for the gates of the fortress that protected "the house," or temple, known in Roman times as Antonia, as well as for the city wall and for Nehemiah's own house, his appointment as governor being presupposed. Keil and Delitzsch likewise take the citadel by the temple to be meant, and dwell on the word pardes as of Aryan origin, denoting in Old Persian the king's pleasure-grounds. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, traces the same word through Arabic and Greek to mean a splendid garden or park, and likens the king's forest to what the New Forest was to William the Conqueror or Windsor to George the Third.

On the closing clause the witnesses are wholly one, and they prize it above all the grants. "And the king granted me, according to the good hand of my God upon me": Clarke marvels that this noble-spirited man ascribes everything to God. He might have said that his long fidelity had earned the king's favour; instead he says only that the king granted his request "because the good hand of my God was upon me" — God favoured him and inclined the king's heart to do what he desired. So the verse ends not in the timber or the letters but in the giver behind the king, the same good hand that had opened the monarch's ear, softened his heart, and would now supply the very beams of the gates. The debate over Lebanon or a park near Jerusalem the witnesses hold lightly; the confession of God's hand they hold fast.
9:
Nehemiah reaches the western provinces and presents his credentials, and the witnesses notice at once the military escort that travels with him. The reformed John Gill wonders who these governors "beyond the river" were, whether the same Tatnai and Shethar-boznai who had held office some eighteen years before, but leaves the question open. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the notice of the captains and horsemen as a supplementary remark, to be taken as a pluperfect — the king "had sent" them with him; and they draw a pointed contrast with Ezra, who had been ashamed to request a military escort from the king, as Ezra 8:22 records, trusting the journey to God alone. To this high officer the king gave a guard of soldiers, who likely remained with him in Jerusalem for his protection; and besides the soldiers, they note, there travelled with him his brethren, whether kinsmen or countrymen.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the escort as both shield and honour. The king appointed captains of the army and horsemen to go with Nehemiah, partly for his safety and partly to show that here was a man whom the king delighted to honour, so that all the king's servants might respect him accordingly. And Henry lifts the observation into a comfort for every servant of God: "those whom the King of kings sends he thus protects, he thus dignifies with a host of angels to attend them." The captains riding beside Nehemiah become an emblem of the unseen guard that convoys those whom God commissions; and the very pomp of his arrival was itself a providence, disposing the country to reckon with him. The escort that honoured him would also, the witnesses note, declare to Sanballat and every watching official that this was no private adventurer to be brushed aside, but the king's own commissioner, whose person the crown itself had undertaken to guard.

The witnesses do not press the small difference between Ezra's way and Nehemiah's into a quarrel. Ezra, going up with a company of returning exiles and a treasure for the temple, had thought it a reproach to ask soldiers of a king to whom he had boasted of his God's protection; Nehemiah, going as a royal governor on the king's own business, received without shame the escort the king pressed upon him. The one refused an escort to honour God before the heathen; the other accepted one because the king's honour and the safety of the work required it — and both, the witnesses imply, acted in faith. Gill leaves the governors nameless, Keil and Delitzsch mark the contrast with Ezra, Henry turns the horsemen into angels; together they bring Nehemiah safely to the edge of the land where his true trials will begin.
10:
No sooner is Nehemiah in the land than his enemies appear, and the witnesses introduce the two adversaries who will shadow the whole book. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark how deeply his coming galled them: it "grieved them exceedingly," the Hebrew doubling the word for evil to strengthen it, that a man was come — Nehemiah reports their vexation with a touch of irony — "to seek the welfare of the children of Israel." Tobiah they take to be styled "the servant," that is, an official of the Persian king, and both men influential chiefs of the hostile nations bordering Judah.

The chief dispute among the witnesses concerns Sanballat's title, "the Horonite." Keil and Delitzsch, with Charles Ellicott, derive it not from Horonaim in Moab — for then he would be called a Moabite — but from one of the two Beth-horons, once of Ephraim and now within the region of Samaria; Ellicott makes him the satrap of Samaria, with Tobiah for his secretary, and observes that Sanballat's name is Babylonian while Tobiah's is Hebrew, and that the revival of Jerusalem would be a blow to Samaria's recent ascendancy. Against this, the reformed John Gill, the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, and John Wesley all take Sanballat to be of Horonaim, a city of Moab, either by birth or by rule; Clarke makes him a Moabite governing the Samaritans under Persia, and Tobiah an Ammonite joint-governor. Wesley reads Tobiah's title "the servant" as marking the low condition from which he had been raised, and finds in a sudden elevation the very reason for his insolence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry looks past the geography to the malice. When Sanballat and Tobiah — Samaritans by station, a Moabite and an Ammonite by birth — saw one come armed with a royal commission to do Israel service, it grieved them to the heart that all their petty arts to weaken Israel were baffled by a generous project to strengthen it. Nothing, Henry says, is a greater vexation to the enemies of good people than to see them cleared of the slanders by which they had been misrepresented to princes, and now not only suffered to live but trusted; "the wicked shall see it, and be grieved." The witnesses part over whether Sanballat came from Moab or from Samaria, but they agree on the man's heart: he could not bear that anyone should seek the good of the children of Israel.
11:
The traveller arrives, and the witnesses pause with him over three quiet days before the work begins. The reformed John Gill reads the rest simply: before entering on any business Nehemiah recovered from the fatigue of the long journey and received the visits of his friends, as Ezra had done on his own arrival, according to Ezra 8:32. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, adds that the three days were "for rest and devotion, after the example of Ezra" — the pause was not idleness but a gathering of body and soul for what lay ahead. The number three, both witnesses imply, is no idle detail: it was long enough to recover strength and to be seen keeping the ordinary courtesies of an arriving governor, and no longer than the urgency of the ruin would allow.

The fuller reading comes from Keil and Delitzsch, also grammatical-historical, who let the three days open toward the night survey that follows. Having rested, Nehemiah arose in the night with a few men to ride round the wall and learn its condition; and the reason he took so small a company, and told no one what his God had put into his heart to do for Jerusalem, was the hostility of Sanballat and Tobiah just named. Though he had come resolved to fortify the city, he spoke of it to no man until he had ascertained by his own eyes the magnitude of the task; he desired to keep his purpose secret until he was certain it could be carried out, and so surveyed the wall by night, with few attendants and those on foot, for secrecy's sake. So much did he weigh the danger that even his own attendants were kept few and his design unspoken, lest a careless word reach the ears already watching for his failure.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very ordinariness of the three days carries their lesson. A man entrusted with a great and dangerous work does not rush at it; he rests, he receives his friends, he keeps his counsel, and he waits for the cover of darkness to take the measure of the ruin before breathing a word of his design. The reverence Ellicott hears in the pause and the prudence Keil and Delitzsch hear in the silence are two sides of the same wisdom: Nehemiah will neither presume upon God by acting rashly nor expose the enterprise to its enemies by speaking prematurely. The three days of rest are the hinge between the journey behind and the survey before, and they show a leader who knows that the first step of a hard task is to be still, to be silent, and to see clearly.
12:
Under cover of night Nehemiah rides out to see for himself, and the witnesses read his secrecy as the wisdom of a prudent builder. The reformed John Gill explains why he chose both the darkness and the small company: it was for greater secrecy, that his business might not yet be known and no schemes be formed to obstruct or discourage it — no schemes, that is, such as his adversaries would gladly have laid had they caught wind of his purpose. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, sharpens the same point — Nehemiah concealed his intentions as long as he could, "knowing that the life of his business lay in secrecy and expedition," and took no beast but the one he rode, to prevent the noise a train of animals would make.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the route and its ruin. He went out by night through the valley-gate, toward the dragon-well and the dung-gate, and viewed the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates consumed with fire; the dragon-well, they suggest, may be the well of Gihon, and the valley-gate the gate leading to the valley of Gihon, near the later Jaffa gate. What Nehemiah rode out to see was not an intact city needing minor repair but a circuit of shattered wall and burned gates.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the practical lessons from the midnight ride. Though the great men of the city took little notice of the newcomer, he took great notice of them and their state, arising in the night to view the ruins, probably by moonlight, that he might see what was to be done and in what method to go about it. "Good work is likely to be well done when it is first well considered." It is the wisdom of those engaged in public business to see with their own eyes, and not to proceed merely on the reports of others, yet to do it without noise and, if possible, unobserved. And Henry adds the spiritual application: those who would build up the church's walls must first take notice of the ruins of those walls, and those who would mend must first inquire what is amiss. Those that shortly are to have the dominion, Henry muses, are for now little known and lie hid, going about their greatest work without observation. The witnesses converge on a single portrait — a leader who tells no one what God has laid on his heart, who trusts his own eyes rather than another's tongue, and who measures the whole extent of the ruin in silence before he asks a single hand to help him repair it.
13:
The witnesses follow Nehemiah's night route gate by gate, fixing the topography of the ruin. The reformed John Gill takes the valley-gate to have led toward the valley of Jehoshaphat, or rather the valley through which the brook Kidron ran, and notes the various roads that issued from it toward Shiloh, Beth-horon, and the country beyond. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, explains the two other landmarks: the "dragon well" was perhaps so called from the figure of a dragon out of whose mouth the stream issued, and the "dung port" was the gate on the eastern side through which the city's filth was carried out into the valley of Hinnom.

Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, sets the same course a little differently. The gate of the valley, he holds, opened on Hinnom to the south of the city; the dragon well is nowhere else mentioned and can no longer be traced; and it was from the dung port, whence offal was taken down to the valley of Hinnom, that Nehemiah surveyed the ruins. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, adds the human detail that the footmen accompanying him directed and led him in the way, since his design was to go round the whole city and observe the compass and condition of the walls and gates, that he might make sufficient provision for the work.

The witnesses do not divide over the essential thing, though they place the gates a little differently on the map. What the verse records, and what they are agreed to underline, is the deliberateness of the reconnaissance: Nehemiah does not glance at one broken stretch and turn back, but sets out to trace the entire circuit, past well and gate and refuse-heap, that his eye may take in the full extent of what has to be rebuilt. The very names — the valley-gate, the dragon-well, the dung-port — are the unglamorous landmarks of a ruined and defenceless town, and Nehemiah rides among them at night precisely so that when he speaks by day he will speak from exact knowledge. The topographical care of the witnesses honours the topographical care of the man: he counted the cost, gate by gate, before he called Jerusalem to build. It is worth marking how the sacred narrative dwells on such humble particulars — a dung-gate, a refuse-valley, a well long since lost — for they are the true measure of a city brought low. There is no glory in the circuit Nehemiah rides, only the evidence of judgment: gates that fire had eaten and walls that lay in heaps. Yet it is exactly here, among the ash and the rubble, that the work of restoration must begin, and the leader who would begin it refuses to look away from a single ruined stone.
14:
The night ride continues to the southern springs, where the ruin at last blocks Nehemiah's path, and the witnesses gather about the pools and the rubble. The reformed John Gill takes the gate of the fountain to have led toward the fountain of Siloah, and the king's pool to be named from it, citing the traveller Rauwolff that the gate of the fountain still stood in his day, so called because it led toward Siloah. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, agrees simply that it is the gate of the fountain of Siloah, also called the king's pool.

Over the identity of that pool the witnesses offer competing guesses. Keil and Delitzsch, also grammatical-historical, place the fountain-gate on the eastern slope of Zion near the pool of Siloah, and identify the king's pool with the reservoir Josephus calls Solomon's pool, east of Siloah, which some have taken for the Fountain of the Virgin, though they weigh the objections carefully — Bertheau, they add, had urged reasons against that identification which they think worth pondering, so that the site cannot be fixed with confidence. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, guesses rather that the king's pool was the aqueduct Hezekiah made to bring the waters of Gihon into the city of David, pointing to 2 Chronicles 32:30.

Where the topography grows uncertain, the witnesses agree on the obstacle that halts him. "There was no place for the beast that was under me to pass": John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, explains it plainly — the way was obstructed with heaps of rubbish, so that the animal could go no farther. The detail is small but eloquent. Nehemiah has come to the part of the circuit where the destruction is worst, where fallen stone and debris choke the narrow path along the ravine, and the very beast that had carried him thus far can find no footing. He must, as the next verse will show, dismount and go up on foot by the brook. The witnesses let the impassable rubble stand as the measure of Jerusalem's desolation: here even a single rider cannot get through, and the man who means to raise the whole wall again first learns, in the dark and on foot, just how far the ruin has gone. Gill and Ellicott name the gate, Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke dispute the pool, Wesley points to the rubbish; together they bring Nehemiah to the hardest yard of his survey. The next verse will find him proceeding on foot up the ravine, so that even the manner of his going — mounted where he could ride, walking where he could not — becomes a parable of a work that must be pressed by whatever means the ruin allows.
15:
The survey reaches its farthest point and turns for home, and the witnesses, few and brief here, trace the last leg of the circuit. The reformed John Gill identifies the "brook" up which Nehemiah went in the night as the brook Kidron, in the ravine along the city's eastern side. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, reads the whole movement as the completion of the round: "the itineration seems to have completed the circuit of the walls," so that Nehemiah, re-entering by the valley-gate from which he had set out, had now seen the entire wall.

Keil and Delitzsch, also grammatical-historical, attend to the Hebrew and correct an old misreading. The construction, they note, expresses a continuous action — Nehemiah kept ascending the valley and viewing the wall; and the words that follow mean simply "I came again into the valley-gate," the verb carrying only the sense of repetition, not, as older expositors thought, that he turned round and retraced by the same road the way he had come. Nehemiah does not detail the latter portion of his circuit, but the plain sense is that he went up the Kidron ravine, surveying as he went, and so returned through the gate by which he had first gone out. They note too that he says nothing of the particulars of this last stretch, having already told enough to show the ruin entire; the record hastens, as Nehemiah himself did, back toward the gate and the rest of his lodging.

The witnesses do not divide, and their very economy suits the moment. The great secret ride is over; the man has gone the whole way round his ruined city under cover of darkness, seen with his own eyes every broken stretch and burned gate, and come back in silence to his lodging with no one the wiser. Gill fixes the brook, Ellicott marks the completed circuit, Keil and Delitzsch settle the grammar of the return; and together they close the night survey exactly as it began, at the valley-gate, with Nehemiah's purpose still locked in his own breast. He has counted the cost in full, and only now — knowing the worst — is he ready to break his silence and lay the work before the people whose hands must do it. The whole survey, taken together across these verses, is a single act of patient love: a man riding and climbing in the dark around a city he had never seen but had wept and prayed over from a palace far away, refusing to trust rumour, refusing to be seen, refusing to speak, until he had measured with his own eyes the full length of its shame. Only such a man, the witnesses imply, is fit to summon others to the labour, for he asks of them nothing he has not first weighed to the last stone.
16:
Back within the walls, Nehemiah still keeps his counsel, and the witnesses probe the secrecy and the officials it was kept from. The reformed John Gill distinguishes the parties: the "rulers" who knew not where he had gone seem to have been officers of the king of Persia, set apart in the verse from the Jewish rulers named alongside the priests and nobles. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the whole company kept in the dark — he had as yet told neither the Jews, nor the priests, nor the nobles (the heads of the great houses), nor the rulers (the town authorities), nor the rest that did the work, that is, the builders; Nehemiah had spoken his purpose to no one at all.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, gives the reason plainly: he made no person privy to his design, that he might hide it as much as possible from their enemies until all was in readiness, lest they take measures to defeat the work. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, judges the caution fully justified by what followed, "for the city teemed with elements of danger," and observes that the nobles and rulers possessed no substantial power to repress opposition, so that their premature knowledge could have helped little and hurt much. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, adds a small grammatical note, that "the rest that did the work" means those whom Nehemiah intended to employ in it — the builders yet to be enlisted.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse rewards their attention with a study in holy discretion. Nehemiah has a royal commission, an escort, and a divine call, yet he breathes his plan to no one — not to the Persian officials who might obstruct it, nor even to the Jewish leaders and priests who would soon embrace it — until he has measured the ruin and matured his design. His silence is neither timidity nor distrust of his people but the prudence of a man who knows how many eyes are watching and how easily a half-formed enterprise is strangled at birth. Only when he can lay the whole matter before them at once, ruin surveyed and remedy proposed, does he mean to speak. Gill sorts the officials, Keil and Delitzsch number those left uninformed, Clarke and Ellicott justify the reticence, Wesley marks the builders to come; together they show that Nehemiah guarded the work in silence until the hour to reveal it had fully come.
17:
The hour of silence ends, and Nehemiah at last lays the ruin and the remedy before the people together. The reformed John Gill takes those he addresses to be the priests and princes of the Jews. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the speech as calculated to win the assembly's favour: setting before them the distress they were in — Jerusalem lying waste and its gates burned — he calls them to build the wall, that they be no more a reproach; and, as the next verse shows, he backs the appeal by telling how God had prospered his undertaking. Charles Ellicott, also grammatical-historical, notes that the "then" carries no fixed note of time: it was when his plans were matured that Nehemiah made his earnest appeal to their patriotism.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the manner of the proposal and finds it a model of leadership. Nehemiah did not undertake the work without them, for it could not be one man's task, nor did he command imperiously, though he held the king's commission; in a friendly, brotherly way he exhorted and stirred them to join with him — "you see the distress we are in, how we lie exposed to our enemies, how justly they reproach us; come, therefore, and let us build up the wall." He spoke of the design, Henry notes, as owing its very origin to the special grace of God, taking no praise to himself but acknowledging that God had put it into his heart; and whatever is of God, Henry adds, ought to be promoted, and those who take it up may hope to prosper, "for what God puts men upon he will own them in."

The witnesses do not divide. What they underline together is the shape of Nehemiah's summons: he neither drives the people as a governor with a warrant nor waits for them to stir themselves, but joins himself to them — "let us build" — and grounds the whole call not in his own authority but in the manifest hand of God and the plain misery before their eyes. The distress is undeniable, the reproach is galling, the remedy is at hand, and the God who moved one heart to plan it will move many to accomplish it. Gill names the hearers, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott mark the timing and the persuasion, Henry the brotherly grace of the appeal; together they show the reproach of a ruined city turned, in a single speech, into the summons to rebuild.
18:
Nehemiah completes his appeal by recounting the providence that had brought him thus far, and the people answer as one. The reformed John Gill glosses "the hand of my God which was good upon me" as the kind providence that had exalted Nehemiah in the Persian court, given him opportunity to lay Jerusalem's case before the king, and inclined the king's heart to grant his request. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, says simply that he opened to them his design and his commission; Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, that he related his providential call, with the king's authority behind it, so that the people were thoroughly enlisted in the good cause.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in their reply the sudden kindling of a whole community. "And they said, Let us rise up and build" — they were ashamed, Henry supposes, that they had sat still so long without attempting so needful a work, and now resolved to bestir themselves and to stir up one another; so they strengthened their hands, their own and each other's, for this good work. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, unfolds the very words: "rise up" means let us do it with vigour, diligence, and resolution, as those determined to go through with it, and "their hands" means their own and one another's.

From the scene Henry draws two abiding truths. First, "many a good work would find hands enough to be laid to it if there were but one good head to lead in it": the people had all seen the desolations of Jerusalem, yet none had proposed the repair until Nehemiah moved it, and it is a pity a good motion should be lost for want of one to make it and break the ice. Second, by stirring up ourselves and one another to what is good, we strengthen ourselves and one another for it, "for the great reason why we are weak in our duty is because we are cold to it, indifferent and unresolved." The witnesses converge on the moment the enterprise truly begins — not when the king signed the commission, nor when Nehemiah surveyed the wall, but when the people, hearing of the good hand of God, caught the resolution from him and made it their own. Gill and Clarke and Ellicott fix the report of providence, Wesley the vigour of the answer, Henry the one head that at last found many hands.
19:
The resolution to build is met at once with scorn, and the witnesses introduce a third enemy and the sneer all three share. The reformed John Gill notes that Geshem the Arabian, now joined to Sanballat and Tobiah, may have been both an Arabian by birth and governor of some part of Arabia near Judea. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark how the adversaries "laughed us to scorn, and despised us," and read the taunt — "What is this thing that ye do? will ye rebel against the king?" — as heavy with irony, for they did not credit the Jews with the power to raise fortifications strong enough to rebel; Geshem, whose fuller name Gashmu appears later, they take for the chief of an Arab tribe dwelling in the south near Jerusalem, as Nehemiah 6:1 and 6:6 attest.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, fastens on the malice hidden under the mockery. The charge "Will ye rebel against the king?" was designed to raise jealousies in the king's mind and so to induce him to recall his ordinance — a shrewd stroke, since the accusation of sedition was the very weapon that had stopped the work before. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, completes the picture of the "triumvirate": they were not independent chieftains, for Tobiah was Sanballat's servant and counsellor and Geshem the leader of an Arabian company mostly in his service; and the account of their contemptuous opposition, given in a few touches, is matched by the contempt with which Nehemiah met it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the scorn in its largest frame. The enemies attempted to discourage the builders on two grounds — representing the work as a silly thing, laughing at them as foolish builders who could never finish what they began, and as a wicked thing, no better than treason, though now the Jews had the king's own commission and were under his protection. And Henry widens the lens: "the enmity of the serpent's seed against the cause of Christ is confined to no age or nation." The church of God, still desolate and exposed, asks our help; and we must not let business or pleasure so engage us that Zion and her welfare are nothing to us. The witnesses do not divide; they name the three mockers, expose the treason they insinuated, and hear in their laughter the ancient and unwearied enmity against every work undertaken for God.
20:
To the enemies' scorn Nehemiah returns a swift and weighty answer, and the witnesses gather about both its confidence and its closing exclusion. The reformed John Gill notes that he answered with spirit and boldness, not at all intimidated by their scoffs or their threats. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the reply with its full gravity — "The God of heaven, he will prosper us; therefore we his servants will arise and build: but ye have no portion, nor right, nor memorial in Jerusalem" — and explain the last word: only members of the congregation, who might hope to live on in their descendants at Jerusalem, could be said to have a "memorial" there.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, unfolds the exclusion. To be a citizen of Jerusalem was a high honour, and the Jews would not permit any who did not belong to the tribes of Israel to dwell there; Nehemiah's words are the very answer Zerubbabel had given the Samaritans in Ezra 4:3, when they offered to share in building the temple. Charles Ellicott, grammatical-historical, reads the whole reply as "a defiance in the name of the God of heaven," and hears in the closing words the implication that these enemies, like the Samaritans of old, really desired a share in the undertaking; Nehemiah makes Zerubbabel's answer but strengthens it — they had nothing in common with Jerusalem, not even a memorial there, save one of shame. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, glosses the three denials: "no portion" means no authority over us nor interest in our church and state, for they were aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and "no memorial" means no monument or testimony of any relation to the place by birth or religion.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the faith beneath the defiance. The Jews bore up themselves with this — that they were the servants of the God of heaven, the only true and living God, that they were acting for him, and that therefore he would bear them out and prosper them, though the heathen raged, as Psalms 2:1 asks why they should. The enemies maligned them, Henry adds, precisely because they had no right in Jerusalem and envied the Jews their right; and so the church's friends may easily despise the impotent menaces of the church's foes. The witnesses close the chapter as one: over against scorn and the threat of accusation, Nehemiah plants his confidence in the God of heaven, claims the city for God's servants alone, and shuts its rebuilding fast against every alien hand.
